guardianfootball.title: Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties yet again to secure Carabao Cup progress
guardianfootball.description: Chelsea must have been resigned to their fate as soon as the shootout arrived at Anfield. Four times they had faced Liverpool on penalties previously and four times they had lost. Number five was confirmed when Wesley Fofana’s wild effort sailed high into the Kop and sent Andoni Iraola’s side into a Carabao Cup quarter-final against his old club Bournemouth. Fofana was not the only culprit as Chelsea’s catalogue of penalty misery against Liverpool gained a new chapter alongside the 2007 Champions League semi-final, the 2019 Uefa Super Cup final and the FA and League Cup finals of 2022. Continue reading...

guardianfootball.title: Arsenal’s Slegers hails ‘role model’ Russo after historic hat-trick sinks Benfica
guardianfootball.description: Alessia Russo wrote herself into the history books once more as she became the highest English goalscorer in the Women’s Champions League. Her hat-trick gave Arsenal a vital 3-0 win against Benfica to send the Gunners up to second in the league phase table. “I’m so happy. I think we’ve found a nice dynamic as well with the last two games,” Russo’s manager, Renée Slegers, said. “She’s one of the leaders and she does it her way. She cares for everyone around her and connects well with her teammates. She leads the way as a role model, doing the right things consistently.” Continue reading...

guardianfootball.description: After Jérémy Doku’s second-half substitute appearance transformed Manchester City into a high-octane proposition, the smart money was on the momentum continuing into a victorious penalty shootout. So it proved as Enzo Maresca’s men triumphed 4-3, Gerónimo Rulli the hero: his save from Lewis Dunk’s fifth spot-kick was decisive, the Argentinean also having repelled Yasin Ayari’s fourth effort. Continue reading...

Kompany’s assistant, Aaron Danks, was in the dugout for Bayern for the last-32 tie, while Harry Kane was rested. The Ballon d’Or winner received a guard of honour from his teammates before kick-off in front of 75,000 fans at the Allianz Arena. Continue reading...

guardianfootball.title: Nketiah takes Crystal Palace past Fulham and earns Sage breathing space
guardianfootball.description: “Can we play you every week?” chanted the Crystal Palace fans as they celebrated a fifth victory over Fulham on their own patch in the space of 18 months. Eddie Nketiah’s first-half goal against the run of play eased some of the growing pressure on Pierre Sage as Palace booked a third consecutive appearance in the quarter-finals of this competition. The good news for Sage is that Arsenal – who beat them on both of those occasions – have already been eliminated . However, he knows that Saturday’s game at Tottenham will have much more bearing on whether he is still around by the time Palace’s Carabao Cup campaign resumes against Sunderland in mid-December. Continue reading...

guardianfootball.description: Even an elite coach would surely struggle at Old Trafford amid the executive chaos and with an unfit, uneven squad In January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity. The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was…

quietus.title: Coming Up for Air: Andy Stott’s Favourite Albums
quietus.description: From 80s synth pop and 90s trip hop through to mischievous, glitched-out electronics, Andy Stott talks through 13 records that hold significance to him ahead of the release of his new album, Late Loop Across a career that now spans more than two decades, Andy Stott’s name has become synonymous with a style of electronic music that is patient and understated. Early records like Passed Me By and Luxury Problems dealt in dubbed-out minimalism and hauntingly gritty chuggers, while albums like 2016’s Too Many Voices and 2019’s It Should Be Us retained some of those qualities while introducing shades of dream pop into his captivating oeuvre. On new record Late Loop, which is his first studio LP…

quietus.title: Prepared for the Future: the Slow Reveal of Aphex Twin’s Drukqs
quietus.description: Drukqs has long been one of John Doran's favourite LPs; with a reissue looming, he attempts to articulate why he loves this critically derided album so much Drukqs by Aphex Twin Rereading the contemporary reviews of Drukqs 25 years later is like rubbernecking the aftermath of a motorway crash. Just ahead of release in October 2001, it became wince-inducingly clear that some previously long-term supporters of Richard D. James were ready to start questioning the validity of his art if not gearing up to fully turn on him. His traditional allies in the leftfield press hated the album, that much was clear. “Too much cake and no nuts” was the stinging but memorable summary minted by Rob Young…

quietus.title: Throwing Muses’ Debut Album Set for 40th Anniversary Reissue
quietus.description: The album has been out-of-print for some time Photo by Andrew Catlin Throwing Muses' self-titled debut album is being reissued to mark its 40th anniversary. The album has been out-of-print for some time, in addition to not being available on streaming services. It marked the first release from the band on 4AD, with the group being the first American signees to the label. The release of Throwing Muses on 4AD in 1986 marked a shift in the label's direction going forward as it looked more significantly towards the American market and signed Pixies via their connection to Throwing Muses not long after. The album went out of print in the early 1990s when plans were made by the band's American…

Rather than participating in online battles (music heads love culture wars more than any other species), I spent most of early autumn listening to college rock trailblazers The Replacements. I somehow missed them in my formative years, but I am now…

Marr is a very affable interviewee though, and given that the conversation was going so well, I couldn’t resist slipping in a cheeky question about how an unnamed “certain person” was chipping away at the legacy of The Smiths with his increasingly unhinged pronouncements. “Honestly? I’m not concerned, is the answer,” he replied, generously. “I’m just not. I’m concerned about so many other things in my day and in the living of my life, you know, that that just isn’t one of my concerns. I go out and play...

aquariumdrunkard.title: Boards of Canada :: Hi Scores
aquariumdrunkard.description: Earlier this year, Boards of Canada unexpectedly released their fifth album Inferno , a case of an influential artist demonstrating that their style remains eminently relatable in 2026 a.d. To close out the year, the group has dipped into its archives, re-releasing the 1996 EP Hi Scores . There’s plenty to savor here, especially for longtime BOC listeners, but there’s also something compelling about being able to hear the group’s roots in such close temporal proximity to their current venture.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Shabazz Palaces
aquariumdrunkard.description: Our guest this week on the show, Ishmael Butler of Shabazz Palaces and Digable Planets, is used to swimming in waters where science fiction weirdness and musical expression mingle. Shabazz Palaces' new album, It’s a Style Sport , represents a new high water mark for the Seattle-based rapper; at once memoiristic and mystical, it’s a strange and beguiling listen. This week, he joins Transmissions host Jason P. Woodbury to discuss basketball, his "Afro-fractal" artistic approach, the influence of artists like the Cocteau Twins, and of course, that goofy old standby: what's it like being a middle aged guy in rap?

aquariumdrunkard.title: All Hallows’ Aquarium Drunkard III
aquariumdrunkard.description: The music of autumn comes in many shades, but none of them without a little smoke and shadow. The days are growing shorter, the air a little cooler, and it is once again time to light the jack-o-lanterns. In our third installment of All Hallows' Aquarium Drunkard , the writers reveal the secrets of their spooky season soundtracks. Inside you'll find doomed teenagers, dissociative episodes, ghost planets, grisly murders and all sorts of monsters, real and imagined. Whatever kind of menace you are looking for, we've got you covered.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Willis Alan Ramsey :: The Aquarium Drunkard Interview
aquariumdrunkard.description: More than 50 years after releasing one of the great cult albums of the early ’70s, Willis Alan Ramsey remains an enigma: a singular songwriter whose long-awaited second record has yet to materialize. But as a recent live appearance and a first-ever vinyl reissue of his self-titled debut attest, Ramsey is very much still here — and already thinking beyond the follow-up he once abandoned. We caught up with the Texas songwriter to talk about the making of a classic, the decades since, and the music still to come.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Surprise Chef :: Frogs In A Pond
aquariumdrunkard.description: Like the best giallo scores, Surprise Chef's Frogs In A Pond finds beauty in the uneasy marriage of the sinister and the seductive. Its analog warmth and locked-in grooves evoke a bygone era without becoming trapped in it, blurring the line between recordings from 2026 and 1976. The eerie mood of the compositions, mixed with the 8-track recording, creates an auditory twilight zone that’s both nostalgic and immediate.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Valerie and Her Week of Wonders :: (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
aquariumdrunkard.description: This Halloween when the usual horror soundtrack fare begins to feel a little too familiar, there is Valerie and Her Week of Wonders. Released in 1970, Jaromil Jireš’s surreal Czech fairy tale is a bizarre, beautiful collision of vampires, witchcraft, religious repression, erotic awakening and dream logic. Paired with Luboš Fišer’s score, the whole thing feels like an intermittent phantasmagoria.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Videodrome :: Psycho II (1983)
aquariumdrunkard.description: About midway through Psycho II (1983), you realize you’re not watching a horror sequel, but a carefully constructed character study. Psycho II isn’t really interested in being a sequel or a horror film; it’s interested in the rehabilitation of Norman Bates, and how those in Bates’ orbit react to that. We may have entered the film expecting a boogeyman, but instead we’re watching a fatally flawed hero, and…we’re rooting for him? Yes, we’re actually rooting for Norman Bates.

mubi.description: One Sings, the Other Doesn't (Agnès Varda, 1977). In her memoir, Varda par Agnès , the French director describes herself as “une féministe de terrain plus qu’une discuteuse,” roughly translated as “a feminist on the ground rather than in theory.” Later in the book, she describes the “feminists” discussing her work, implying that she was outside this group. How feminist she reads from any angle now is unclear. Many would, for instance, find her focus on the body and childbirth essentialist. Her 1975 short, Réponse de femmes: Notre corps, notre sexe ( Women Reply: Our Bodies, Our Sex ), opens with this prompt: “What does it mean to be a woman?” The text is painted on glass and held up by two…

A few months earlier, the same film had world premiered at Cannes, in the Un Certain Regard section, and walked away with a special mention for the Caméra d’Or. It was the first Nigerian film to be programmed in the official selection at the festival. Variety called Akinola Davies Jr.’s film miraculous. Rotten Tomatoes aggregated the critical assessment as 98% positive. However, there exists a cultural invisibility at home that stands against these genuine international recognitions. Despite all these…

Born in 1939 in Kyushu, Japan, he moved to Tokyo to attend Nihon University, coming of age during the turbulent protests against the renewal of the mutual security treaty between Japan and the United States in 1959–60. He started making films with a student group and soon emerged as one of the leading figures in the burgeoning underground cinema scene. In the mid-1960s, Adachi became involved with the sexploitation industry, writing and directing several striking examples of the genre for Koji Wakamatsu’s production company.
